source.title: Is your batch size the problem? Revisiting the Adam-SGD gap in language modeling
source.authors: Teodora Srećković; Jonas Geiping; Antonio Orvieto

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff affecting the reported findings.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests and refines the claim that adaptive optimizers often outperform SGD: it finds that the gap depends strongly on batch size, tuning, and training duration, and that tuned SGD can match or outperform Adam in some language-model settings.
record.gate_note: The study's direct results concern optimizer performance and batch-size sensitivity in language modeling. It does not test random-label memorization, natural-label generalization, convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Figure-only trajectories are retained as figure-only without estimating values from plotted curves.
record.test_reason: Held-out perplexity comparisons test V4 and V5 in Transformer language-model pretraining. Momentum and learning rates are tuned, so this does not reproduce V4's limited-tuning protocol. Fixed-token comparisons test V5's fixed-data-budget condition; fixed-step comparisons alone do not.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: carefully tuned momentum SGD can compete with Adam at small batches, whereas large batches expose SGD's slower progress per step. The authors report competitiveness up to 1B parameters and argue that batch size and gradient noise constrain explanations of the optimizer gap. Figure 5 itself establishes training performance; held-out scale comparisons appear separately in Figure 14.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies tuned Adam versus momentum SGD in Transformer language-model pretraining, with batch-size and training-duration sweeps. It uses no weight decay and generally applies global gradient norm clipping; it does not reproduce the image-classification or generalization-gap methods in the cited optimizer studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, number of training steps/token budget, dataset, model size/depth, momentum, learning rate, clipping choice, and Hessian heterogeneity affect the reported optimizer-performance gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Training perplexity can favor SGD after sufficiently long small-batch training, including at 410M and 1B parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small batches and sufficient training can make momentum SGD competitive with Adam in Transformer optimization.

fits_no_version.finding: Large-batch SGD has a larger training-perplexity deficit on rare tokens; the pattern disappears at small batches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size moderates the relationship between token frequency and the Adam-SGD optimization gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient correlation and directional sharpness track successful training trajectories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Update alignment and directional curvature characterize optimizer progress in the tested Transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger batches benefit Adam and SignSGD more than SGD on noisy quadratics, with Hessian heterogeneity amplifying the gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer batch-size sensitivity can arise in quadratic optimization without a generalization comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: Grafting Adam's direction onto SGD's magnitude approaches Adam's training performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Update direction contributes more than magnitude to the tested large-batch SGD optimization deficit.

fits_no_version.finding: Clipping large momentum coordinates reduces SGD's training-perplexity deficit without fully matching Adam.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive momentum clipping can improve large-batch SGD optimization.

record.peer_reviewed: Short version accepted at the 2025 HiLD Workshop at ICML; preprint under review
record.problems: Most optimizer comparisons report perplexity, not a training-versus-test error gap. Several batch-size and scale results are presented only in figures without numerical values in the supplied text. Some plotted large-scale comparisons show training perplexity rather than held-out performance.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only intermediate optimizer curves, gradient norm clipping frequency, warmup-length sweep, and clipped-coordinate fractions by layer were omitted because they do not provide a distinct held-out optimizer-performance result mapped to these versions, or are measurements of mechanisms rather than the version's named performance outcome. Appendix figures for other batch sizes repeat the reported trend without numerical text values.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and corresponding natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

The learning-rate-and-schedule-only tuning protocol; image classification; equal-training-performance comparisons; switching optimizers; weight-decay interventions; the specific word-level language-model setting.

Image classifiers; normalization and regularization interventions; controlled tests of warmup or learning-rate scaling as remedies; whether additional training restores large-batch held-out performance to the small-batch level.
Dropout interventions and their interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally sized random removals.

missing.what: Final held-out perplexity comparisons across learning rates for the 410M and 1B models. R8 and R9 capture training trajectories only. Figure 14 explicitly supplies validation outcomes; their optimizer ordering and values need extraction before assigning scale-specific generalization verdicts.

record.verdict_notes: The extraction's tranche rationale incorrectly describes the claim as adaptive optimizers often outperforming SGD. V4 instead presents an SGD advantage with explicit qualifications. No challenges label is assigned because these experiments tune momentum as well as learning rate, and V4 already allows broader tuning to reverse the ranking. Fixed steps must not be treated as fixed epochs or fixed tokens.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier generalization.
Image-classification benchmarks, language-model Adam advantages over SGD under broader tuning, weight-decay effects, and switching from Adam to SGD.
Whether image classifiers can match small-batch accuracy within the same epoch budget, and the effects of normalization changes.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.check: Adam has lower held-out perplexity: 28.77 versus SGD's 30.76. This reverses V4's headline SGD advantage, although broader tuning and language modeling already qualify that headline. For V5, this row supplies the small-batch reference for R2 and R3; it cannot independently establish a batch penalty.

conditions.value: various; up to 160k for batch 16 and 20k for batch 128

rows.measure: Training perplexity trajectory; held-out perplexity trajectories are shown in figures.
rows.note: The authors state that the optimizer gap decreases with longer training and SGD outperforms Adam at the maximum small-batch training duration; precise plotted values are not stated.

rows.subject: 160M-parameter nanoGPT model
rows.operation_detail: Compare optimizer performance across batch sizes under a fixed token budget and a fixed-step regime.

conditions.value: 2.5k to 160k, with larger batches not run for the largest step counts

rows.measure: Validation perplexity across batch sizes and training durations.
rows.note: Text states that at fixed token budget the gap increases with batch size and SGD degrades as batch grows; with more steps SGD improves and can match or outperform Adam. Curves are not numerically tabulated.
rows.check: This aggregates opposing condition groups. For V4, Adam leads at larger batches, while sufficiently long small-batch training permits SGD to match or outperform it. For V5, the fixed-token panel shows SGD worsening with batch size but Adam improving up to a critical size. The fixed-step panel does not hold the data budget fixed. Split these distinctions in interpretation without inventing numerical values.

source_check.correct: Split conditions: V4 has an Adam advantage at larger batches and an SGD match or advantage with sufficiently long small-batch training. For V5, fixed-token SGD performance degrades with batch size, whereas Adam improves up to a critical batch size. Fixed-step comparisons alone do not establish V5.

rows.subject: 160M-parameter nanoGPT model
rows.operation_detail: Measure perplexity by token-frequency group during training for Adam and SGD at small and large batch sizes.

conditions.value: 10 groups, from least frequent 10% to most frequent 10%

rows.note: Authors report a larger SGD deficit for rare tokens at large batch, while this effect is absent at small batch; values are not tabulated.
rows.check: Figure 7 concerns per-frequency-group perplexity during training; the supplied text does not establish a held-out evaluation for these groups. It cannot establish V4's generalization comparison.

rows.subject: 160M-parameter nanoGPT model
rows.operation_detail: Measure gradient correlation and directional sharpness along training updates for Adam and SGD.
rows.measure: Gradient correlation, directional sharpness, and their sum as a second-order loss-change approximation.
rows.note: Authors state the metrics align with success or failure but do not directly explain the optimizer gap.
rows.check: Gradient alignment and directional curvature measure optimization dynamics, not held-out optimizer performance. They also do not measure V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance or its correlation with generalization gaps.

rows.subject: Toy quadratic models
rows.size_stated: 9-dimensional quadratic; Hessian eigenvalues stated in Appendix D
rows.operation_detail: Train SGD with momentum, SignSGD with momentum, and Adam on homogeneous and heterogeneous quadratic objectives at batch sizes 1 and 5.

conditions.value: homogeneous or heterogeneous; same eigenvalue spectrum

rows.uncertainty: mean and 2-sigma standard deviation for 10 runs
rows.note: Text reports that Adam benefits from increasing batch size in both Hessian settings, SGD does not seem to profit, and heterogeneity amplifies the gap. Values are not tabulated.
rows.check: Quadratic training loss measures optimization rather than held-out generalization. Neither V4 nor V5 is established by this experiment.

rows.subject: 160M-parameter nanoGPT model
rows.operation_detail: Graft optimizer update directions and magnitudes in both combinations at large batch; tune learning rates.

conditions.value: SGD magnitude with Adam direction (SGD#Adam), and Adam magnitude with SGD direction (Adam#SGD)

rows.baseline: Adam and SGD trajectories, figure only
rows.value: SGD#Adam performs comparably to Adam; Adam#SGD behaves similarly to SGD, figure only
rows.note: The authors interpret the results as indicating that update direction is the more problematic component of SGD at large batch.
rows.check: This grafting ablation reports training perplexity and compares modified optimizer updates. It does not establish V4's held-out performance outcome.

rows.subject: 160M-parameter nanoGPT model
rows.operation_detail: Apply adaptive momentum clipping to the largest fraction of momentum coordinates; tune learning rate.
rows.value: Adaptive clipping with 10% performs best and reduces the gap; it does not fully match Adam, figure only

rows.check: This adaptive-clipping ablation reports training perplexity. Its improvement over baseline SGD does not establish a held-out optimizer comparison.
